property_summary: For any caller that is not the (current) owner, calling transferOwnership must revert and leave `owner` unchanged; the mutant lets anyone set `owner` to a nonzero value, breaking the invariant that a non-owner call cannot change `owner`.

For any caller allowed by onlyOwner, transferOwnership(newOwner) must set owner to exactly newOwner; the mutant sets owner to msg.sender instead, so owner != newOwner for any newOwner different from the caller.
After the owner transfers ownership to a nonzero address, c.owner() must equal exactly that address; the mutant stores address(0) instead, breaking this for every nonzero newOwner.

For any caller equal to the current owner (and any newOwner), transferOwnership must set the owner to newOwner; the mutant inverts the require so the owner's own call reverts and the owner is unchanged.

property_summary: For any caller that is not the current owner, transferOwnership must revert and leave the owner unchanged; the mutant inverts the require so such a call succeeds and changes owner.
For any address actor, calling owned() from actor succeeds exactly when actor is the current owner (onlyOwner enforces this); the mutant makes owned() revert even for the owner, breaking the rule.

After ownership is transferred to any fuzzed address, calling owned() from that new owner must succeed (onlyOwner permits the current owner); the mutant reverts owned() unconditionally, so it fails for every new owner.

For every actor address a, after ownership is transferred to a, a call to owned() from a succeeds on the reference C (only the owner may execute), whereas the inverted mutant makes the owner's call revert.
For any caller that is not the current owner, calling `owned` must revert (onlyOwner access control); deleting the require lets any caller succeed, breaking the rule for some fuzzed actor.

For any admissible newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) as the current owner sets c.owner() to exactly newOwner; the buggy version never updates owner, so for any newOwner != address(0) the getter returns the old owner instead.

For every non-owner caller (owner is initially address(0), so any non-zero caller), transferOwnership must revert and leave ownership unchanged; the mutant removed the onlyOwner require, so it lets a non-owner succeed, breaking the rule.

For any admissible caller (initial owner is address(0), so anyone passes onlyOwner) and any newOwner address, transferOwnership must set the owner to exactly newOwner; the mutant sets owner to address(this) instead, so for any fuzzed newOwner != address(this) the rule is violated.

For any admissible caller and newOwner (newOwner != address(this)), transferOwnership must set owner to exactly newOwner; the mutant sets owner to address(this) instead, violating this for some input.

For any caller, a successful call to owned() must not change the owner (the onlyOwner gate guarantees msg.sender==owner, and the body is empty), so owner stays at the value set by transferOwnership; the mutant writes owner=msg.sender inside owned(), so the owner value diverges for some inputs.

For every fuzzed address, once the owner transfers ownership to that address, only that address may invoke owned() and the owner recorded by c must remain exactly that address (calls by anyone else revert and leave it untouched); the mutant's extra owner = msg.sender write breaks the invariant that owned() is a pure no-op for the legitimate owner's session state.

For any admissible input, transferring ownership to newOwner (via the owner) makes c.owner() a fixed value that no subsequent attempt at owned()—whether by the owner (where the body is empty) or by any other address (which reverts at onlyOwner)—can ever change; the mutant's unconditional owner = msg.sender write inside owned() makes c.owner() diverge for some input.
